Chapter.Content: Reading map · Previous chapter · Next chapter
A texture stores samples of a signal over a surface, and its footprint changes with projection. Filtering must account for that changing footprint to avoid unstable detail and aliasing.
By the end: Connect texture sampling, surface footprints and filtering choices.
Recall question: Why does a minified texture need a different footprint than a magnified one?
Match a texture footprint to the surface signal

Implementation-specific passages retain observations from the supplied Kairo/Maveb snapshot. They are not a fresh audit of those repositories. Source exercises and illustrative code are teaching material; only explicitly recorded checks have been executed here.

Chapter.Content: If those equations, their units/domains, and their corresponding Kairo code paths can be reconstructed, M115/M116 are genuinely understood rather than vocabulary-memorized.
Textures attach spatially varying signals to surfaces, so filtering must follow their projected footprint.
Texture is a function over a surface

A texture map stores a signal in a two-dimensional parameter domain. A surface point is assigned UV coordinates ((u,v)), and the renderer samples the image or function there. Parameterization is the mapping that flattens a surface to a domain; it inevitably introduces distortion, seams, or both. For a mesh triangle with per-vertex coordinates (u_i,v_i), barycentric interpolation transfers a hit point to texture space. If texture coordinates are outside the unit tile, the sampler needs a policy: repeat, clamp, mirror, or border color.
A sampled texture usually needs interpolation. If the query lies between four texel centers with fractional coordinates , bilinear interpolation blends horizontally and then vertically:

For instance, if the four texel values are 0, 1, 1, and 0 in row order, then at the center (a=b=0.5) the two horizontal interpolants are both 0.5, so the final result is 0.5. Nearest-neighbor sampling would instead jump between 0 and 1 at texel boundaries. Bilinear filtering removes that discontinuity, although it cannot recover detail that was lost when the image was sampled.

This produces a continuous-looking signal from discrete texels, but it is still a reconstruction filter. The texture lecture discusses parameterization, texture lookup, and bilinear interpolation, then connects shaders to procedural signals such as Perlin noise MITG-14 (00:25:00–00:45:00; 00:45:00–01:05:00). Procedural textures evaluate a function instead of storing every value, making them resolution-independent and useful for irregular natural patterns. Their high-frequency detail still has to be filtered when projected to a pixel grid.
Texture coordinates make one surface address many kinds of detail

A triangle mesh describes where a surface is, but that is too coarse a storage scheme for fine color, roughness, or relief. Texture mapping gives each surface point a second address in a two-dimensional parameter domain. For a triangle with 3D corners and corresponding texture corners , a hit point has barycentric weights , with and . Reuse those weights in texture space:

The mesh intersection answers where the ray hit in 3D; the second expression answers which texel neighborhood to sample. If has weights , then the texture lookup is exactly the same weighted average of the three texture corners. This is why texture coordinates are attached to triangle corners rather than inferred from world position. A shared 3D vertex may have two different UV coordinates on opposite sides of a seam. If one vertex had to have only one UV address, seams could not open. MITG-14 (00:15:34–00:21:04)

A UV atlas cuts a curved surface into patches before laying it flat. A triangle itself is planar and can be flattened without stretching, but the neighborhood around a curved vertex generally cannot be flattened while preserving every length and angle. A closed sphere cannot be continuously mapped to one flat disk without a cut or singularity. A designer therefore balances distortion against seam placement: seams hidden behind ears or under a character may be visually safer than a mathematically uniform cut. Leaving more edges connected improves continuity, but concentrates distortion; cutting every triangle removes much of that distortion while producing many discontinuous islands and difficult painting. MITG-14 (00:21:46–00:25:58; 00:35:42–00:36:48)

UV generation is an optimization problem with both geometric and topological choices. Even with the cuts fixed, each mesh vertex contributes two unknowns. A local objective can penalize edge stretch or angle distortion. But a valid atlas must also avoid unintended overlap: if two unrelated triangles occupy the same UV region, they sample the same texture colors. The lecture’s Tutte construction fixes the boundary to a convex shape and places each interior UV point at a weighted average of its neighbors. Each condition is linear, so all interior positions can be solved as a sparse linear system. This gives a useful injective starting map under the method’s assumptions; later optimization may trade cut length against local distortion while preserving non-overlap. MITG-14 (00:40:22–00:48:52)

Parameterization methods include artist-chosen seams, closed-form cylinder or sphere projections, and automatic optimization. A photo projected from a virtual camera is useful for image-based rendering, where a simple geometric proxy carries photographs from one or more views. It is less suitable for a freely turning object because a projection designed for one camera may stretch or slide under another. A tiled texture can reuse a small image with wraparound coordinates, while a normal map stores a perturbed normal rather than color. Normal mapping gives a low-polygon mesh fine shading variation, often baked from a high-resolution model, but cannot produce the true silhouette, parallax, or mutual occlusion of displaced geometry. MITG-14 (00:37:49–00:40:20; 00:49:49–00:56:41)

A sampled image is a grid of texels (texture pixels), so a non-integer UV coordinate needs reconstruction. Nearest-neighbor lookup picks one texel and creates visible jumps. Bilinear filtering interpolates between four neighbors: interpolate horizontally in the two rows, then vertically between the results. The order gives the same bilinear polynomial. When the texture becomes small on screen, one output pixel covers many texture texels. Sampling only one can alias the pattern into flicker or moiré. A mip pyramid precomputes successively half-sized averages; selecting the level whose texel footprint roughly matches the screen footprint approximates the needed area average. The extra memory is bounded: for a square texture, the level sizes sum to , ignoring tiny rounding effects. A surface tilted away from the camera has an elongated, direction-dependent footprint, so isotropic mip selection can blur too much in one direction; anisotropic filtering samples that footprint more selectively. MITG-14 (00:27:06–00:34:15)

Texture maps can hold any per-surface signal, not just RGB: diffuse coefficient, specular strength, roughness, or other BRDF parameters. Normal maps encode direction changes that perturb the normal used by lighting. Store directions in a coordinate frame that rotates with the surface (often tangent space), rather than naïvely storing world-space XYZ values that become invalid when the object moves. A coarse mesh with a normal map can reproduce the lighting of fine bumps from a distance, while remaining visibly flat in silhouette or when occlusion matters. MITG-14 (00:49:49–00:56:41)

A procedural shader computes a surface signal from position or other attributes at shading time. For example, a checker can be built from parity of integer cell coordinates, so it extends indefinitely and has no stored image boundary. Procedural patterns offer compact, resolution-independent definitions, but they still require filtering: a mathematically sharp checkerboard can alias when many cells fall into one pixel. Perlin noise supplies smooth, locally varying values with a controllable spatial scale. Combining octaves at different frequencies creates multiscale structure; thresholding or taking absolute values introduces ridges, and perturbing a sinusoid with noise creates irregular marble veins. These are design functions, not physical laws. MITG-14 (00:57:07–01:13:44)
